title: How Computers Work
sub: Bits, bytes, text encodings, processes, system calls and how the shell finds a command
goals: Convert numbers between binary, decimal and hexadecimal by hand and in code
Explain how text is stored as bytes in ASCII and UTF-8
Describe what the kernel, a process, a system call and a file descriptor are
Tell a terminal from a shell and a compiled program from a script
Predict which program runs when you type a command, using PATH and exit status

blocks.text: Everything you will do in this book, from reading a packet capture to scanning a port, comes down to bytes moving between programs, and every program is a process asking a kernel to do things on its behalf. In this chapter you will learn to read and write those bytes in binary and hexadecimal, dump a file as hex to see what is really inside it, and follow the path from the key you press to the program that runs. By the end you will predict which `python3` will start before you type it.

Keep Terminal open. The sections alternate between a concept and something to run, and the tools for looking at bytes (`xxd`, `od`, `hexdump`, `bc`) get their reference cards in the middle of the chapter.
Bits, bytes and hexadecimal

A **bit** is one binary digit, 0 or 1. It is the smallest unit a computer stores, because hardware represents it as one of two voltages or magnetic states. A **byte** is 8 bits, and the term **octet** means exactly the same thing, which is why networking documents prefer it. One byte holds 2^8 = 256 distinct values, 0 to 255.
Binary is a positional system like decimal, with powers of two instead of powers of ten. Each bit position carries a weight, and the value of a byte is the sum of the weights of the bits that are 1:

Writing eight 1s and 0s for every byte is tiring, so people use **hexadecimal** (base 16). It has sixteen digits, `0` to `9` and `a` to `f`, and one hex digit stands for exactly four bits (a **nibble**). So one byte is always two hex digits, and conversion needs no arithmetic: split the byte into two nibbles and translate each.

Take 202 again: `1100 1010` is nibble `1100` = c and nibble `1010` = a, so 202 = `0xca`. The prefixes `0x` (hex), `0b` (binary) and `0o` (octal in Python; a leading `0` in C, bash and `/usr/bin/printf`, but not in zsh arithmetic by default) tell a reader which base a literal is in. Hex appears constantly in this book: MAC addresses, IPv6 addresses, the `0xffffff00` netmask that `ifconfig` prints, packet dumps, memory addresses and checksums.
Try the same conversions in Python. The in-page runner is the quickest calculator you have:

Edit the code to convert your own numbers. `bin()`, `oct()` and `hex()` return strings with a prefix; `int(text, base)` parses text in a given base; the format specs `08b` and `02x` mean "binary, zero-padded to 8" and "hex, zero-padded to 2".
Powers of two worth knowing

head: Power
Value
Where it appears
rows: values in a byte, an octet of an IPv4 address
the number of TCP and UDP ports (0 to 65535)
the size of the IPv4 address space
the number of possible MAC addresses
the size of the IPv6 address space

blocks.text: Storage vendors, macOS Finder and networking use powers of 1000: 1 MB is 1,000,000 bytes and 100 Mbit/s is 100,000,000 bits per second. Memory and some tools (`ls -lh`, `du -h`) use powers of 1024. The binary names are KiB, MiB and GiB. Bandwidth is quoted in **bits** per second and file sizes in **bytes**, so a 100 Mbit/s link moves at most 12.5 MB/s.
An IP address is four bytes (and one number)

An IPv4 address such as `192.168.1.23` is four octets written in decimal and separated by dots, which is a convenience for people. The network sees one 32-bit number. Shift each octet into its place and combine them:

blocks.code:
ip = "192.168.1.23"
octets = [int(x) for x in ip.split(".")]
print(octets)
print(" ".join(f"{o:08b}" for o in octets))
print(".".join(f"{o:02x}" for o in octets))
value = (octets[0] << 24) | (octets[1] << 16) | (octets[2] << 8) | octets[3]
print(value, hex(value))

blocks.text: `<<` shifts bits left (a shift by 8 multiplies by 256, moving an octet one place up) and `|` combines bits. The same number, `0xc0a80117`, is what appears in a packet dump. [Addressing and subnets](#addressing) builds subnetting on exactly these operations.
Text is numbers: ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8
A computer stores text by agreeing on a number for each character. **ASCII**, from the 1960s, defines 128 characters using the values 0 to 127 (7 bits):

items.text: **0 to 31 and 127** are control characters. The ones you meet daily: 9 is tab, 10 is **LF** (line feed, the newline on macOS and Linux), 13 is **CR** (carriage return), 27 is ESC.
**32** is the space, and **33 to 126** are the printable symbols.
**48 to 57** are the digits `0` to `9`, **65 to 90** are `A` to `Z`, and **97 to 122** are `a` to `z`.

blocks.text: Upper and lower case differ by exactly 32, which is a single bit (bit 5, `0x20`): flipping it changes the case. Digits are not the numbers they show: the character `7` is the byte 55 (`0x37`), and converting between the two is a subtraction of 48.

blocks.code:
for ch in "Aa0 ~\n":
    print(repr(ch), ord(ch), hex(ord(ch)), f"{ord(ch):08b}")
print(chr(72), chr(0x69), "".join(chr(c) for c in (72, 101, 108, 108, 111)))
print(ord("a") - ord("A"), chr(ord("g") ^ 0x20), chr(ord("G") ^ 0x20))

blocks.text: `ord(c)` turns a character into its number and `chr(n)` goes back. The last line uses `^` (XOR) with `0x20` to flip case. A line ending is also just bytes: macOS and Linux end lines with LF (`0a`), Windows files use CR LF (`0d 0a`), and HTTP uses CR LF too, which you will see when you speak HTTP by hand.
Unicode and UTF-8

ASCII has no `é`, `€` or `漢`. **Unicode** assigns a **code point** (written `U+20AC`) to over a million characters. A code point is still just a number, so a separate rule, an **encoding**, says how to turn it into bytes. The dominant one is **UTF-8**, which uses 1 to 4 bytes per character and has two useful properties: ASCII text is byte-for-byte identical in UTF-8, and the first byte tells you how many bytes follow.

blocks.code:
for s in ("A", "é", "€", "𝄞"):
    b = s.encode("utf-8")
    print(f"{s}  U+{ord(s):04X}  {len(b)} byte(s)  {b.hex(' ')}")
print(len("café"), len("café".encode()))
print(bytes([72, 101, 108, 108, 111]).decode())
blocks.out:
A  U+0041  1 byte(s)  41
é  U+00E9  2 byte(s)  c3 a9
€  U+20AC  3 byte(s)  e2 82 ac
𝄞  U+1D11E  4 byte(s)  f0 9d 84 9e
4 5
Hello

blocks.text: `"café"` is 4 characters but 5 bytes, because `é` takes two. A program that confuses characters with bytes breaks on non-English text; Python keeps them apart (`str` versus `bytes`), and [Python basics](#py-basics) returns to this. Decoding bytes that are not valid UTF-8 raises an error, shown here on purpose:

blocks.code: b"\xff\xfe".decode("utf-8")

blocks.text: The message reads `UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xff in position 0: invalid start byte`, because `0xff` can never start a UTF-8 character.
Signed numbers, byte order and bit operations
Negative numbers: two's complement

Hardware has no minus sign, so signed integers reuse the same bits. In **two's complement** the top bit counts as a large negative weight: in 8 bits, the weights are -128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. The pattern `11111111` is therefore -128 + 127 = -1, and the range of a signed byte is -128 to 127. To negate a number, invert all bits and add 1. Addition then works the same for signed and unsigned values, which is why every modern CPU uses this scheme.

blocks.code:
for n in (5, -5, -1, -128):
    print(f"{n:>4}  8-bit pattern {n & 0xFF:08b}  unsigned {n & 0xFF}")
print(int.from_bytes(b"\xff", "big", signed=True), int.from_bytes(b"\xff", "big"))
print((255 + 1) & 0xFF)
blocks.out:
5  8-bit pattern 00000101  unsigned 5
  -5  8-bit pattern 11111011  unsigned 251
  -1  8-bit pattern 11111111  unsigned 255
-128  8-bit pattern 10000000  unsigned 128
-1 255
0

blocks.text: The same byte, `ff`, is 255 or -1 depending on how you interpret it. The last line shows **overflow**: in 8 bits, 255 + 1 wraps to 0. Fixed-size integers wrap silently, and the shell uses 64-bit integers:

The second result shows 2 to the 63rd power already wrapped to the most negative 64-bit number, and the third shows 2 to the 64th wrapping all the way to 0. Python integers grow as needed, so the same calculation there gives `18446744073709551616`. Remember the difference when you do arithmetic in a script.
Byte order (endianness)

A number wider than one byte must be laid out in memory in some order. **Big-endian** stores the most significant byte first, the way people write numbers. **Little-endian** stores the least significant byte first. Apple Silicon and Intel Macs are both little-endian, but the internet is big-endian: protocol headers carry multi-byte fields most significant byte first, called **network byte order**. Port 8080 is `0x1f90`, so it travels as the bytes `1f 90`.

blocks.code:
import sys
port = 8080
print(hex(port), port.to_bytes(2, "big").hex(), port.to_bytes(2, "little").hex())
print(sys.byteorder)
print(int.from_bytes(bytes.fromhex("1f90"), "big"))

blocks.text: Reading `1f90` as little-endian would give `0x901f`, or 36895, a classic bug when parsing packets by hand. In [Python for networking](#py-net) the `struct` module's `!` format character means network byte order.
Bit operations
Six operators work on individual bits, and they are how masks, flags and addresses are manipulated:

tokens.exp: AND: keep a bit only where both operands have a 1
255.255.255.0 as a number, 24 ones followed by 8 zeros

blocks.text: The classic use is a **mask**. ANDing an address with a netmask keeps the network part and zeroes the host part. Using the number from earlier:

blocks.code:
addr = 0xC0A80117
mask = 0xFFFFFF00
net = addr & mask
print(hex(net), ".".join(str((net >> s) & 0xFF) for s in (24, 16, 8, 0)))
print(f"{mask:032b}")
print(bin(mask).count("1"))
print(addr & ~mask & 0xFFFFFFFF)

blocks.text: `192.168.1.23` with mask `255.255.255.0` gives network `192.168.1.0`. The mask has 24 leading ones, so it is written `/24`, and inverting it and ANDing gives the host part, 23. Every subnet calculation in the book is this operation.
Tools for looking at bytes
Files and network traffic are bytes. These tools show them as hex. All of them ship with macOS except where noted, and they all read stdin, so they sit at the end of pipelines.

blocks.name: xxd
blocks.sum: Make a hex dump of a file or of standard input, or turn a hex dump back into bytes.

how.text: `xxd` reads bytes and prints them in rows: an offset, the bytes in hexadecimal grouped in pairs, and on the right the same bytes as ASCII, with `.` standing for anything unprintable. Because it shows ASCII beside the hex, you can find text inside binary data at a glance.

Plain mode (`-p`) prints only hex with no offsets or ASCII, and `-r` reverses a dump back into raw bytes, so `xxd -p` and `xxd -r -p` convert in both directions. This is a convenient way to type binary data on the command line.

Reverse: read a hex dump and write the bytes. With `-p` the input is plain hex.
Stop after N bytes.
Start at byte offset N (negative values count from the end).
Show N bytes per row (default 16).
Group N bytes between spaces (default 2; `-g 1` puts a space between every byte).
Show bits (binary digits) instead of hex.
Use upper-case hex digits.

gotchas: `echo` appends a newline (`0a`), so `echo Hello | xxd` shows six bytes. Use `printf 'Hello'` or `echo -n` for exactly five.

blocks.name: od
blocks.sum: Dump a file in octal, hexadecimal, decimal or character form.

how.text: `od` ("octal dump") is the oldest dump tool and the most flexible. `-t` chooses how each unit is shown: `x1` is hex bytes, `u1` is unsigned decimal bytes, `o1` is octal bytes, and `-c` shows characters with C-style escapes such as `\n`. `-A` chooses how offsets are shown (`x` for hex, `d` for decimal, `n` for none), and `-An` is what makes `od` ideal for feeding plain numbers to other tools.

Show each byte as 2-digit hex (`u1` unsigned decimal, `o1` octal).
Show each byte as a character or escape (`\n`, `\0`).
Read only n bytes.
Skip n bytes first.
Do not collapse repeated rows into `*`.

examples.code: printf 'ABC' | od -An -tu1 | tr -s ' ' '\n' | awk '{s += $1} END {print s}'

gotchas: Without `-v`, `od` replaces identical consecutive rows with a lone `*`. That is easy to miss when counting bytes.
GNU `od` (Linux) accepts a `z` suffix for an ASCII column; the BSD `od` on macOS does not. Use `xxd` or `hexdump -C` for a combined view.

blocks.name: hexdump
blocks.sum: Print a file in hexadecimal with `-C`, the canonical hex plus ASCII layout.

how.text: The BSD `hexdump` shipped with macOS prints 16 bytes per row. Without options it uses an old 16-bit word format that is hard to read on little-endian machines, so almost everyone uses `-C`, which shows an offset, two groups of eight bytes and an ASCII column between bars. The final line is the total length in hex.

gotchas: The default format without `-C` prints 16-bit little-endian words, so the bytes of `Hello` appear as `6548 6c6c 006f`. Use `-C` to see them in file order.

blocks.name: printf (numbers)
blocks.sum: Print formatted text, which makes it the dependable tool for converting numbers between bases.

how.text: `printf` fills conversion specifications in its format string with its arguments. For numbers, `%d` prints decimal, `%x` and `%X` print hex (lower and upper case), `%o` prints octal, and a width such as `%08d` pads with zeros. Arguments that start with `0x` are read as hex, so `printf '%d\n' 0xff` prints 255. A leading `0` means octal in bash and in `/usr/bin/printf`, but zsh's builtin `printf` reads `010` as decimal 10 unless the `OCTAL_ZEROES` option is set. Unlike `echo`, it adds no newline and interprets backslash escapes in the format the same way everywhere, including `\x41` for a byte.
zsh also does base conversion inside arithmetic: `$(( 16#ff ))` reads hex, `$(( 2#101 ))` reads binary, and `$(( [##16] 255 ))` prints in hex.

flags.d: Signed decimal integer.
Hex, lower or upper case.

gotchas: `printf '%d' 0xff` works only because the shell's `printf` understands the prefix. Python's `int("0xff")` raises `ValueError`; pass a base: `int("0xff", 16)`, or `int("0xff", 0)` to honour the prefix.

blocks.name: bc
blocks.sum: An arbitrary-precision calculator that reads expressions from stdin and converts between bases.

how.text: `bc` evaluates expressions line by line. `ibase` sets the base used for input and `obase` the base used for output, which makes it a quick converter: set `obase=2`, type a decimal number, and read the binary. `scale=N` sets the number of decimal places for division, because `bc` does integer division by default. `-l` loads a math library and sets `scale` to 20.

gotchas: Set `obase` before `ibase`. After `ibase=16`, the digits `10` mean sixteen, so `ibase=16; obase=10` sets the output base to 16 and does nothing visible.
Hex digits must be upper case in `bc`; `ibase=16; ca` is read as variables, not as a number.

blocks.name: strings
blocks.sum: Print the runs of printable characters found inside a binary file.

how.text: `strings` scans a file for sequences of at least four printable ASCII characters (the default minimum) and prints each on its own line. It is a quick way to find text hidden in a binary: error messages, URLs, host names, version numbers. Because it only reads, it is safe to point at anything.

blocks.name: file (first look)
blocks.sum: Identify what kind of data a file contains by examining its contents, not its name.

how.text: `file` compares the start of a file against a database of signatures called magic numbers (for example `#!` at the start of a script, or the Mach-O header at the start of a macOS program) and falls back to examining whether the bytes look like text. A file named `photo.jpg` that holds a script is reported as a script. The extension is only a hint to humans and to Finder.

blocks.text: Run `printf 'Hello, world!\n' | xxd`, then `head -c 64 ~/lab/access.log | xxd`, then `head -c 32 /bin/ls | xxd`. The first two are text, so the ASCII column is readable. The third is a program: the first four bytes are a magic number that tells the kernel what format the file is in.
The machine: CPU, memory and disk
Three components do most of the work, and the gap in speed between them explains a great deal of system behavior.

items.text: The **CPU** executes instructions: tiny operations such as add, compare, load, store and jump, billions per second per core. It keeps its working values in a handful of **registers** and a small, very fast **cache**. A modern Mac CPU has several cores, each able to run a separate stream of instructions.

**RAM** (memory) holds the programs and data currently in use. It is fast and **volatile**: it forgets everything at power-off. Every byte has a numeric **address**, and the CPU reads and writes by address. On Apple Silicon the CPU and GPU share one pool, called unified memory.
**Storage** (an SSD on any current Mac) keeps data permanently in files arranged by a **filesystem**; macOS uses APFS. It is slower than RAM by about three orders of magnitude.

blocks.text: Each step down is far slower than the one above it. Scaling one nanosecond up to one second makes the gaps vivid:

blocks.code:
latencies = [("L1 cache", 1e-9), ("RAM", 100e-9), ("SSD read", 100e-6),
             ("LAN round trip", 1e-3), ("Internet round trip", 50e-3)]
for name, secs in latencies:
    scaled = secs / 1e-9
    print(f"{name:<20} {scaled:>12,.0f} s  = {scaled / 86400:>8.2f} days")
blocks.out:
L1 cache                        1 s  =     0.00 days
RAM                           100 s  =     0.00 days
SSD read                  100,000 s  =     1.16 days
LAN round trip          1,000,000 s  =    11.57 days
Internet round trip    50,000,000 s  =   578.70 days

blocks.text: The figures are typical orders of magnitude, not measurements of your Mac. If a cache access took one second, an internet round trip would take about a year and a half. This is why programs read data in big blocks, why caching is everywhere (browsers, DNS, ARP, the CPU), and why network latency, not bandwidth, so often decides how fast something feels.
Ask your Mac about itself. All of these are read-only:

blocks.code:
$ uname -m
arm64
$ sw_vers -productVersion
27.2
$ sysctl -n machdep.cpu.brand_string
Apple M2 Pro
$ sysctl -n hw.ncpu
12
$ sysctl hw.memsize | awk '{printf "%.0f GiB\n", $2/1024/1024/1024}'
16 GiB

blocks.text: `uname -m` reports the CPU architecture: `arm64` for Apple Silicon, `x86_64` for Intel. `sysctl` reads kernel settings by name, and `awk` turns a byte count into GiB. The [System and processes](#system) chapter covers these commands in full.
The kernel, processes and system calls

Programs do not touch hardware. Between them and the hardware sits the **kernel**, the privileged core of the operating system. macOS's kernel is called XNU (a Mach microkernel plus BSD Unix components). It has three jobs that matter here: it **shares the hardware** between programs, it **isolates** programs from each other, and it **provides services** such as files and network connections.

The CPU enforces the split. Code in **user space** (every program you run) can compute but cannot read arbitrary memory or talk to devices. Code in **kernel space** can do anything. A program that needs a service executes a special instruction that transfers control to the kernel; that request is a **system call**.

blocks.code:
⟪c:user space⟫    curl:  connect(sock, addr)           your program asks
   ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
                     libSystem wrapper function           C library
                             │  trap (svc on arm64, syscall on x86_64)
   ═══════════════════════════▼═══════════════════════════  kernel boundary
   ⟪r:kernel space⟫  XNU: check arguments and permissions
                     TCP/IP stack ──▶ Wi-Fi driver ──▶ radio

blocks.text: Common system calls and what they do:

head: Call
Purpose
Seen when you...
rows: Get or release a handle to a file or device
`cat` a file, or `curl` receives a page
Create a copy of a process; replace its program
Wait for a child; finish with a status
Send a signal to a process
Map a file or memory into the address space

blocks.text: Networking is not a special case: a TCP connection is created with `socket` and `connect`, and data moves with `write` and `read`, the same calls used for files. Section 2 of the manual documents them (`man 2 intro`, `man 2 socket`).

A **process** is a running instance of a program. The kernel gives each one a **process ID** (PID), a private **virtual address space** (so one process cannot see another's memory), a table of open files, a current directory, a user identity and an **environment**. On macOS, process 1 is `launchd`, the first process, which starts and supervises everything else.

blocks.name: ps (first look)
blocks.sum: List processes: their IDs, parents, owners and commands.

how.text: `ps` reads the kernel's process table and prints a snapshot. With no options it shows only the processes attached to your current terminal. `-A` (or `-e`) selects every process, and `-o` chooses the columns: `pid`, `ppid` (parent PID), `user`, `comm` (the command name), `%cpu`, `%mem`, `etime` (time running). Appending `=` to a field name (`-o pid=`) removes its heading, which is useful when another command will read the output.
macOS `ps` accepts both the BSD style (`ps aux`) and the System V style (`ps -ef`). The [System and processes](#system) chapter covers it in depth.

gotchas: A `ps | grep name` also matches the `grep` itself. Use `pgrep name` (see [System and processes](#system)) or the bracket trick `grep '[n]ame'`.

blocks.text: Every process has a **parent**: the process that created it. When you type a command, your shell uses `fork` to make a copy of itself, the copy uses `execve` to replace its program with the one you asked for, and the original waits. When the child finishes, it returns an **exit status** that the shell stores. Two variables expose this: `$$` is the shell's own PID and `$PPID` is its parent's.

blocks.code:
$ echo "my PID is $$"
my PID is 2473
$ zsh -c 'echo "child PID is $$ and its parent is $PPID"'
child PID is 2478 and its parent is 2473

blocks.text: (Your PIDs will differ.) The child's parent is the shell that launched it, which shows the rule: each command you run is a child of your shell.

On Linux, `strace` prints every system call a program makes. macOS has no `strace`. `dtruss` (built on DTrace) exists, but System Integrity Protection blocks it for most programs, and `sudo fs_usage -w -f network` shows a live, read-only stream of network activity per process. You do not need either for this book, but knowing that every network tool is a thin layer over `socket`, `connect`, `write` and `read` explains why they all behave alike.
Everything is a file

The Unix design idea with the largest consequences is that very different things are accessed through the same small interface: **open** a name to get a number, then **read** and **write** bytes through that number. Regular files, directories, hardware devices, pipes and network sockets all work this way.

The number is a **file descriptor** (fd), a small integer that indexes a per-process table of open things. Every process starts with three: 0 is standard input, 1 is standard output and 2 is standard error. The next `open` gets 3. That is why `>` and `2>` in [Streams, redirection and pipes](#pipes) can rewire a program without the program knowing: the shell changes what fd 1 points to before the program starts.

blocks.code:
$ lsof -p $$ | head -6
COMMAND  PID USER   FD   TYPE DEVICE SIZE/OFF NODE NAME
zsh      612  you  cwd    DIR   1,16      640 ... /Users/you
zsh      612  you  txt    REG   1,16  1360688 ... /bin/zsh
zsh      612  you    0u   CHR  16,0 0t1038220 ... /dev/ttys000
zsh      612  you    1u   CHR  16,0 0t1038220 ... /dev/ttys000
zsh      612  you    2u   CHR  16,0 0t1038220 ... /dev/ttys000

blocks.text: Your shell's fds 0, 1 and 2 are all open on one **device file**, `/dev/ttys000` (the exact name differs per Terminal tab), a character device ("CHR"). Device files live in `/dev`, and a few are worth knowing:

An endless supply of random bytes
The terminal of the current process

blocks.text: `ls -l` tells you what kind of thing a name is with the first character of its mode string: `-` regular file, `d` directory, `l` symbolic link, `c` character device, `b` block device, `s` socket, `p` named pipe.

blocks.code:
$ ls -l /dev/null
crw-rw-rw-  1 root  wheel    0x3000002 Oct  8 09:12 /dev/null
$ tty
/dev/ttys000

blocks.text: Terminal, shell and TTY
People use "terminal", "shell" and "console" interchangeably, and the confusion hides how the pieces cooperate. There are three distinct parts:

items.text: The **terminal emulator** (the Terminal app) is only a window. It draws text and turns key presses into bytes.

The **TTY** (from "teletype") is a kernel device that sits between them. A **pseudo-terminal** is its software form: a pair of connected ends, one held by the Terminal app and the other appearing to programs as `/dev/ttys000`. The TTY handles line editing basics and translates special keys: it turns [[⌃C]] into an interrupt signal for the foreground program, and [[⌃D]] into end-of-input.
The **shell** (zsh) reads a line from the TTY, expands it, starts programs and waits for them. It is just another program, and you can start a different shell inside it by typing `bash` or `zsh`.

blocks.text: You can inspect the interrupt character the TTY is configured with:

blocks.code:
$ stty -a | grep -o 'intr = [^;]*'
intr = ^C

blocks.text: When you SSH into another machine, the same layering reappears: your Terminal talks to a local pseudo-terminal, `ssh` forwards the bytes across the network, and a remote pseudo-terminal feeds a remote shell. Knowing the parts makes sense of `ssh -t`, of `tmux`, and of why a remote program can ask you for a password without the shell ever seeing it.
Programs: compiled, interpreted, scripts
A CPU only runs **machine code**, the instructions for its architecture. Programs reach that form in different ways:

items.text: **Compiled** languages (C, Rust, Go, Swift) are translated ahead of time into a machine-code **executable**. On macOS the format is **Mach-O**. It runs directly and fast, but only on the architecture it was built for (`arm64` or `x86_64`; some files are "universal" and contain both).

**Interpreted** languages (zsh, Python) are executed by another program, an **interpreter**, which reads the source and does what it says. Python first compiles source into a compact **bytecode** (cached in `__pycache__`) that a virtual machine runs.

A **script** is a text file for an interpreter. It starts with a **shebang**, the two characters `#!` followed by the interpreter's path. When you run a script, the kernel's `execve` sees `#!` in the first two bytes and starts that interpreter with the script as its argument.

blocks.code:
$ printf '#!/bin/zsh\necho "hello from $0"\n' > /tmp/hello.zsh
$ chmod +x /tmp/hello.zsh
$ /tmp/hello.zsh
hello from /tmp/hello.zsh
$ head -c 2 /tmp/hello.zsh | xxd
00000000: 2321                                     #!

blocks.text: `chmod +x` sets the execute permission (covered in [Files and permissions](#files)), and `xxd` shows the two bytes `23 21` that the kernel looks for. Use `file` to see which kind a file is:

blocks.code:
$ file ~/lab/README.txt /bin/ls /tmp/hello.zsh
/Users/you/lab/README.txt: ASCII text
/bin/ls: Mach-O universal binary with 2 architectures: [x86_64:Mach-O 64-bit executable x86_64] [arm64e:Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64e]
/tmp/hello.zsh: a /bin/zsh script text executable, ASCII text

blocks.text: `README.txt` is plain text, `/bin/ls` is compiled, and the script is text that names an interpreter. Your Mac's exact wording may differ. Intel-only programs run on Apple Silicon through Rosetta translation, which is why `uname -m` and `arch` matter when a tool misbehaves (the [Fixes](#fixes) chapter has the details).
Environment variables and PATH

Each process carries an **environment**: a set of `NAME=value` strings the kernel copies into every child it starts. Programs read it for configuration (`HOME`, `USER`, `LANG`, `PATH`, `EDITOR`). Look at yours:

blocks.name: printenv
blocks.sum: Print environment variables, one named variable or all of them.

how.text: `printenv` shows the environment of the process it runs in, which is inherited from your shell. Given a name it prints only that variable's value (and exits non-zero if it is not set); with no arguments it prints every `NAME=value` pair. It prints only **exported** variables. A shell variable you set without `export` is not part of the environment and does not appear.

examples.desc: One variable
Everything, sorted
Find every variable whose value mentions a folder
Show variables as names only

gotchas: `printenv NAME` exits with status 1 when the variable is unset, which makes it usable in `if` tests in scripts.

blocks.name: env (first look)
blocks.sum: Run a program with a modified environment, or print the environment when given no program.

how.text: With no command, `env` prints the environment, like `printenv`. With a command, it first changes the environment for that one command and then runs it: `name=value` sets or overrides a variable, and `-i` starts from an empty environment. It leaves your shell untouched, which makes it the right tool to test how a program behaves under different settings.

flags.d: Start with an empty environment.
Remove NAME from the environment for this command (BSD and GNU).

examples.desc: Run one command with a changed variable
Check what a clean environment contains

gotchas: `env -i` removes `PATH` too, so inside it you must name programs by their full paths.

tokens.exp: set MY_VAR to temp for this single command only
run the following string as commands and exit
the command string; the single quotes keep the outer shell from expanding $MY_VAR, so the child shell does it

blocks.text: Shell variables versus environment variables

Variables you set in the shell are private to it. To pass one to the programs you start, you must **export** it, which adds it to the environment those children inherit. A one-off assignment placed in front of a command sets it for that command only.

blocks.code:
$ MY_VAR=hello
$ echo "$MY_VAR"
hello
$ zsh -c 'echo "child sees: [$MY_VAR]"'
child sees: []
$ export MY_VAR
$ zsh -c 'echo "child sees: [$MY_VAR]"'
child sees: [hello]
$ MY_VAR=temp zsh -c 'echo "inline: [$MY_VAR]"'
inline: [temp]
$ echo "$MY_VAR"
hello

blocks.text: The child process, a new copy of zsh, saw nothing until the variable was exported, and the inline form changed it for one command without touching the shell's own copy. Children cannot change their parent's environment, which is why `cd` and `export` inside a script do not affect your Terminal after the script ends.
How the shell finds a command
When you type a word at the start of a command line, zsh has to decide what it means. It checks, in this order:

blocks.code:
1. reserved word    if  for  while  [[  {  function
   2. alias            alias ll='ls -l'
   3. function         defined in your startup files or scripts
   4. builtin          cd  echo  export  print  type  (run inside the shell itself)
   5. external program searched in the PATH folders, left to right, first match wins

blocks.text: A word that contains a slash (`./run.sh`, `/bin/ls`) skips the search and names the file directly. External programs are found through **`PATH`**, a colon-separated list of folders. The shell remembers where it found each command in a hash table so that it need not search again, and it forgets when `PATH` changes.

blocks.code:
$ echo $PATH
/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin
$ type ls
ls is /bin/ls
$ which ls
/bin/ls

blocks.text: `type name` reports how the shell would interpret the name (alias, builtin, function or file). Where several matches exist, `type -a` lists all of them in search order:

blocks.code:
$ type -a python3
python3 is /opt/homebrew/bin/python3
python3 is /usr/bin/python3
$ echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | nl
     1	/opt/homebrew/bin
     2	/opt/homebrew/sbin
     3	/usr/local/bin
     4	/System/Cryptexes/App/usr/bin
     5	/usr/bin
     6	/bin
     7	/usr/sbin
     8	/sbin

blocks.text: Homebrew's folders come first, so Homebrew's `python3` wins over Apple's. The folder order is the entire explanation of "why does `python3` run the wrong one".

`/etc/zprofile` runs a helper called `path_helper` for login shells. It reads the folders listed in `/etc/paths` and every file in `/etc/paths.d/`, and puts them in `PATH`. Your own `~/.zprofile`, which runs afterward, adds Homebrew in front. Apps launched from the Dock or Finder do not inherit your shell's `PATH`, which is why a GUI app can fail to find a tool that works in Terminal.
Exit status

When a process ends, it hands the kernel a number from 0 to 255, its **exit status**. The shell keeps the last one in the variable `$?`. By long convention **0 means success** and any non-zero value means failure, with the specific number free for the program to choose. `&&`, `||` and `if` all branch on it.

blocks.name: echo $?
blocks.sum: Print the exit status of the previous command: 0 for success, non-zero for failure.

how.text: After every foreground command the shell stores its exit status in the special parameter `$?`. Because `echo $?` is itself a command, it sets `$?` again, so read the status immediately after the command you care about, or copy it first with `rc=$?`. Programs choose their codes, but a few are conventional, and the shell reserves some: 126 means found but not executable, 127 means command not found, and 128 plus N means killed by signal N, so 130 is [[⌃C]].

examples.desc: A command that succeeds, and one that fails
examples.code:
grep -q root /etc/passwd; echo $?
grep -q zzzzz /etc/passwd; echo $?

examples.desc: A command the shell cannot find
Print a verdict from the status
Keep the status for later, after printing something else

gotchas: In a pipeline `$?` holds only the last command's status. zsh's `pipestatus` array has every stage, covered in [Streams, redirection and pipes](#pipes).

Meaning

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Dotted address to binary

task.text: Write `ip_to_bin(ip)` that converts a dotted IPv4 address into its four 8-bit binary groups joined by dots, for example `"192.168.1.23"` becomes `"11000000.10101000.00000001.00010111"`. Then write `ip_to_int(ip)` that returns the same address as one integer.

why.text: Splitting on dots gives four decimal strings. `int()` converts each to a number and the format spec `08b` renders it as 8 binary digits padded with zeros. For the single integer, each step shifts what you have so far left by 8 bits and ORs in the next octet, which is the same positional rule as building a decimal number digit by digit.

blocks.title: Flip the case with one bit

task.text: Write `flip_case(text)` that swaps upper and lower case for every ASCII letter and leaves every other character unchanged, using only `ord`, `chr` and the XOR operator (`^`), not `str.swapcase`. For example `flip_case("Hello, Net 42!")` is `"hELLO, nET 42!"`.

why.text: Letters differ in case by exactly bit 5 (value 32), so XOR with `0x20` toggles it. XOR only on the letter ranges, because `@`, `[`, backtick and `{` sit next to those ranges and would be turned into other symbols. Testing the boundaries (the last assertion) is a habit worth building.

blocks.check:
assert flip_case("Hello, Net 42!") == "hELLO, nET 42!", "flip_case('Hello, Net 42!') should be 'hELLO, nET 42!'"
assert flip_case("") == "", "empty string stays empty"
assert flip_case("abcXYZ") == "ABCxyz", "abcXYZ becomes ABCxyz"
assert flip_case("@[`{") == "@[`{", "characters next to the letter ranges must not change"

blocks.title: Decode a hex dump of "Hello"

items.text: Print the bytes of the five-character string `Hello` with `xxd`, with `od -A x -t x1` and with `hexdump -C`. Compare the three layouts.
Dump `echo Hello` and find the extra byte. Which character is it?
Convert the plain hex string `48656c6c6f2c206e6574776f726b210a` back to text with `xxd -r -p`.
Write the decimal ASCII values of `Hello` using `od -An -tu1`.

hints: `printf 'Hello'` prints without a trailing newline; `echo Hello` adds one.
For step 3, pipe `echo` into `xxd -r -p`. For step 4, use `-An` to suppress the offsets.
blocks.solution:
printf 'Hello' | xxd
printf 'Hello' | od -A x -t x1
printf 'Hello' | hexdump -C
echo Hello | xxd
echo 48656c6c6f2c206e6574776f726b210a | xxd -r -p
printf 'Hello' | od -An -tu1

why.text: `H` is 0x48 (72), `e` 0x65 (101), `l` 0x6c (108) twice and `o` 0x6f (111). The extra byte from `echo` is `0a`, the LF newline. The hex string in step 3 spells `Hello, network!` followed by a newline. All three dump tools show the same bytes with different decoration; knowing how to read each lets you work on any machine.

blocks.title: Which python3 runs?

task.text: Find out, using only shell commands, which `python3` your shell starts, which others exist and in what order the folders of `PATH` are searched. Then print the path of the interpreter from inside Python itself and check that it matches.

hints: `type -a` lists every match in search order. `tr` can turn the colons of `PATH` into newlines.
Inside Python, `sys.executable` holds the path of the running interpreter.
blocks.solution:
type -a python3
echo $PATH | tr ':' '\n' | nl
python3 -c 'import sys; print(sys.executable)'

why.text: The first match of `python3` along `PATH` wins, and `type -a` shows all of them. Python's own report should name the same file, or a file that `command -v python3` links to; if `sys.executable` points into a different folder, a symlink or a wrapper is involved. Checking this before debugging "wrong version" problems saves a lot of time.

blocks.title: A subshell with its own PATH

tokens.exp: start a subshell: a child shell, so changes die when it ends
set PATH inside the subshell to a folder that holds nothing
look this command up using the new PATH
end of subshell; the real shell's PATH was never touched

blocks.title: Break PATH on purpose, then fix it

task.text: In a subshell (parentheses start a child shell, so nothing leaks into your real one), set `PATH` to a folder that does not exist and run `ls`. Read the error and print its exit status. Then repeat with `PATH=/bin` so that it works, and once more with `PATH=/nonexistent` but calling `/bin/ls` by its full path.

hints: `(PATH=/nonexistent; ls)` runs inside parentheses. Print the status with `echo $?` right after.
A command that contains a slash is never looked up in `PATH`.

why.text: With a bad `PATH` zsh finds no `ls` and prints `command not found: ls`, exit status 127. `/bin` contains `ls`, so setting it fixes the lookup. A full path bypasses the search entirely, which is the standard way to run a program when `PATH` is broken. (Do not add `| head` inside the subshell: `head` lives in `/usr/bin`, which the shortened `PATH=/bin` does not contain, so the pipeline would fail at its second stage.) The subshell is why the change vanishes at the closing parenthesis: a child's environment never reaches its parent.

blocks.title: Walk up the process tree

task.text: Starting from your shell (`$$`), print the PID, parent PID and command name of each ancestor, one line per process, until you reach PID 1. Use a loop and `ps -o` with headings suppressed.

hints: `ps -o pid=,ppid=,comm= -p N` prints one line for process N with no heading.
Update the variable with `pid=$(ps -o ppid= -p $pid | tr -d ' ')` each time round, and stop when `pid` reaches 1.
blocks.solution:
pid=$$
while [[ $pid -gt 1 ]]; do ps -o pid=,ppid=,comm= -p $pid; pid=$(ps -o ppid= -p $pid | tr -d ' '); done
ps -o pid=,ppid=,comm= -p 1

why.text: Each line gives the parent of the previous one: your shell, the `login` process that started it, the Terminal app, and finally `launchd`, PID 1, the ancestor of everything. `ps -o ppid=` prints only the parent's PID, `tr -d ' '` strips the padding BSD `ps` adds, and the loop follows the chain. Seeing the tree makes "every command is a child of your shell" concrete.

questions.why: Two hex digits give 16 x 16 = 256 values; `ff` is the largest, 15 x 16 + 15 = 255, which is eight 1 bits.

questions.q: How many bytes does the euro sign `€` take in UTF-8?
questions.why: U+20AC lies between U+0800 and U+FFFF, so it uses the three-byte pattern: `e2 82 ac`. ASCII characters take one byte, and the characters in U+0080 to U+07FF take two.

questions.q: Port 8080 is 0x1f90. In what order do those bytes travel in a TCP header (network byte order)?
questions.why: Network byte order is big-endian: the most significant byte goes first, so `1f` then `90`. A little-endian machine stores it as `90 1f` in memory and must swap it when building packets.

questions.q: In zsh you run `MY_VAR=hello` and then `zsh -c 'echo $MY_VAR'`. What prints?

options.text: An empty line, because the variable was not exported

questions.why: Only exported variables are copied into a child's environment. `export MY_VAR` would change the result, and `MY_VAR=hello zsh -c ...` sets it for that single command.

questions.q: Which exit status means "command not found"?
questions.why: The shell uses 127 for a command that does not exist in `PATH` and 126 for a file that is found but not executable. 130 is a command killed with Ctrl-C.

questions.q: When you type `python3`, in what order does zsh look?

options.text: Reserved words, aliases, functions, builtins, and finally PATH folders from left to right
Alphabetically through all folders on the disk

questions.why: Aliases and functions take priority over builtins, which take priority over external programs. Among external programs the first match in `PATH` wins, which is why folder order decides which `python3` runs.

You now know what is inside a file, a process and a command line. Continue to [How networks work](#networks) to follow those bytes across a wire, from an Ethernet frame to a web page.
